Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Justice Department officials blocked liberals and people with Democratic Party ties from a highly selective program that funneled young lawyers into government jobs, according to an internal investigation released Tuesday. A bias against liberals existed in a Justice program meant to hire young lawyers, an investigation found. Esther Slater McDonald, a political appointee at the Justice Department, "wrote disparaging statements about the candidates' liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis," said the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine. McDonald, who has left the department, refused to be interviewed for the investigation. The report, the first official investigation to document politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration, is an offshoot of the larger investigation of Justice Department politics triggered by the furor over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys. It found two of three members of a screening committee considered political views and experience when choosing new lawyers for the Justice Department Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program. The report found that McDonald and Michael Elston, the chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, engaged in misconduct, an administrative violation. The third member of the screening committee, career lawyer Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in the politicization of the process. Elston was interviewed by the investigators, who asked him about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing the selection process. Elston told investigators he could not recall Goodling telling him to select lawyers who appeared to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales' philosophy. Goodling testified before a House panel last year that she had told Elston he should identify such candidates. Goodling directed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006. She and Elston have both left the Justice Department. She refused to be interviewed for the inspector general's report. As a result of the controversy, the hiring process was changed in 2007 to insulate hiring decisions from political considerations. Both Justice Department policy and federal law prohibit discrimination in hiring for career positions on the basis of political affiliations. The report did not find clear evidence that an earlier screening committee took political considerations into account. It says data from 2002 shows a disparity in the hiring of liberal and conservative candidates, but there were no complaints about the committee's work from 2003 to 2006, when Goodling put Elston in charge of the process. The report Tuesday is the first of perhaps several to be issued as the broad-ranging investigation into the role partisan politics has played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Goodling is expected to be a central figure in later inspector general reports examining efforts to increase the influence of conservatives in the department. The Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct, joined in the inspector general's investigation. CNN's Terry Frieden contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON** — A Justice Department inspector general report released Wednesday found that political and ideological considerations improperly influenced the hiring process for the department's prestigious Honors Program during the Bush administration, in violation of federal law and department policy.

The report, the result of a lengthy investigation by Inspector General Glenn A. Fine, concluded that senior political appointees screened candidates for the highly competitive program — traditionally reserved for top law school graduates — based on their perceived political affiliations, including membership in organizations such as the Federalist Society or the American Constitution Society, as well as past work for Democratic or Republican politicians.

The Honors Program has long been considered a prized entry point into the Justice Department, allowing new attorneys to bypass the normal hiring process used for career positions elsewhere in government. Traditionally, hiring decisions were left to career attorneys within each division based on merit, academic achievement, and legal writing samples.

According to the report, that changed during the Bush administration, when political appointees in the department's leadership began reviewing candidates' resumes for clues about their ideological leanings. Investigators found that some qualified candidates were rejected or downgraded because of perceived liberal affiliations, while others with conservative credentials were favored — regardless of their qualifications.

"Our investigation found that the process was tainted by improper political and ideological considerations that likely resulted in some qualified candidates not being hired," Fine wrote in the report, adding that such practices violated federal civil service laws barring discrimination based on political affiliation in hiring for career positions.

The findings echo earlier controversies surrounding the Bush Justice Department, including a 2008 inspector general report that found similar political vetting had occurred in the hiring of career prosecutors and immigration judges. That report led to criticism of then-Attorney General Alberto Gonzales and several senior aides, some of whom resigned amid the fallout.

Wednesday's report specifically scrutinizes the role of the department's Office of Attorney General and the now-defunct screening committee that reviewed Honors Program applications starting in 2002. Investigators said the committee, made up largely of political appointees, at times used internet searches to look for information about applicants' political leanings, including searches for terms associated with liberal organizations or Democratic campaigns.

Several career officials interviewed by investigators said they raised concerns at the time about the politicization of the hiring process but were overruled or ignored by superiors.

The Justice Department, now under the leadership of Attorney General Eric Holder, said in a statement that it had already implemented reforms to ensure that hiring for the Honors Program and other career positions is based solely on merit. Officials said the recommendations from the inspector general's report would be reviewed and additional safeguards put in place if necessary.

Legal experts said the findings, while covering a period that ended with the change in administrations in 2009, underscore lingering concerns about the politicization of career civil service positions at the Justice Department.

"This is a reminder of how important it is to have a firewall between political leadership and career hiring decisions," said one former Justice Department official who worked in the Civil Rights Division and was not authorized to speak publicly. "Once that firewall breaks down, it undermines public confidence in the fairness and independence of the department."

Congressional Democrats had pushed for the inspector general's investigation following earlier revelations of political interference in hiring practices during the Bush years. Some lawmakers said Wednesday's findings should prompt further oversight hearings.

The inspector general's report does not name individual officials responsible for the flawed hiring practices, but noted that at least some conduct might warrant further internal review by the department.

The Honors Program has since undergone significant changes, with the department instituting new safeguards intended to insulate the hiring process from political influence.

**WASHINGTON (AP)** — The Justice Department is facing renewed scrutiny following allegations that political appointees improperly screened job candidates based on perceived liberal affiliations, in violation of federal civil service laws that bar such considerations in career hiring decisions.

The allegations, detailed in findings from the department's Office of Inspector General and Office of Professional Responsibility, center on hiring practices for career positions — including slots in the department's prestigious Honors Program and summer internships — that by law are supposed to be filled without regard to political ideology.

Investigators found that some officials used internet searches, resume keywords and interview questions to identify candidates' political leanings, then used that information to reject applicants deemed insufficiently conservative, according to the report.

"Using political or ideological affiliations to make employment decisions with respect to career attorney positions is not merely wrong, but also is inconsistent with the Department's commitment to the rule of law," the report concluded.

According to the findings, one senior official reviewed candidates' resumes for indications of ties to Democratic politicians, liberal organizations or law school affiliations perceived as left-leaning. Membership in organizations such as the American Constitution Society — widely viewed as a liberal counterpart to the conservative Federalist Society — was cited in some cases as a factor working against applicants.

Investigators also said some qualified candidates with strong academic and professional credentials were passed over, while less-qualified applicants with perceived conservative credentials were selected instead.

**DEPARTMENT RESPONSE**

A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency takes the findings seriously and has instituted new hiring safeguards, including standardized interview questions, mandatory training on hiring laws for supervisors, and closer oversight of the Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program selection process.

"The department is committed to ensuring that hiring for career positions is conducted solely on the basis of merit," the spokesperson said in a statement.

**REACTION**

Lawmakers on the House and Senate Judiciary Committees said they planned to press department leadership for additional information at upcoming oversight hearings.

"The Justice Department exists to enforce the law without fear or favor," said one senior member of the Senate Judiciary Committee. "When hiring decisions are made based on partisan litmus tests rather than qualifications, it undermines public trust in the institution."

Legal advocacy groups on both sides of the aisle called for accountability, though they differed on the appropriate remedy. Some urged referrals for possible disciplinary action against officials involved, while others cautioned against what they described as an overcorrection that could chill legitimate consideration of candidates' judicial philosophy for policy-related, non-career positions.

**BACKGROUND**

Federal law and Justice Department policy generally prohibit political or ideological considerations in hiring for career civil service positions, as opposed to political appointee positions, which are exempt from such restrictions. The distinction is intended to preserve the department's independence and ensure continuity across administrations of different parties.

The Office of Inspector General said it would continue to monitor the department's implementation of corrective measures and provide periodic updates to Congress.

*This story will be updated as more details become available.*

Conversely, affiliations with conservative or Republican-linked organizations were not treated as negative factors in the same way.

The findings echo earlier concerns raised during the 2007 controversy over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys, which prompted congressional investigations into whether the dismissals were motivated by the prosecutors' unwillingness to pursue cases perceived as politically beneficial to Republicans, or their handling of politically sensitive investigations.

The report calls for reforms to insulate the hiring process from political interference, including restoring greater authority to career officials in evaluating candidates and implementing safeguards to prevent political or ideological factors from influencing personnel decisions in the future.

Justice Department officials have acknowledged the need for corrective measures and indicated that changes to hiring protocols have already been implemented to prevent similar issues from recurring in future hiring cycles.
